newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa pumps first crude from offshore oil wells.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa pumps first crude from offshore oil wells.

text.p: South Africa's first "black gold" flowed out of the Oribi oilfield about 140km (80 nautical miles) southwest of Mossel Bay at first light on Monday and officials said they hoped to pump 20,000 barrels of crude a day.

The $75 million project, 80 percent state-owned and 20 percent owned by Energy Africa Ltd oil company, began production more than two months behind schedule mainly because bad weather held up the refurbishment of the Orca production rig, the officials said.

South Africa has searched for oil for more than 20 years and has been converting gas found off Mossel Bay into petrol for some years, but Monday's flow was the first commercial production of crude oil in the country's history.

The new production platform is expected to meet around five percent of South Africa's daily crude oil requirement. Sasol Ltd's oil-from-coal plants provide over 30 percent of the country's liquid fuel requirement.
The oil is being pumped into a 700,000-barrel shuttle tanker, which will take about a month to fill.
The first cargo will be ferried to the Caltex Oil SA refinery in Cape Town, which has agreed to take the oil field's initial 600,000 barrels.
The second cargo will go to a refinery in Durban.

For the last few weeks, engineers from the state's majority-owner Soekor have been overseeing the reopening of three exploratory wells and connections to the rig customised to serve as a floating production platform.
The Oribi oilfield is expected to produce enough oil a day to meet around five percent of South Africa's daily needs. This amount will taper off gradually over three to six years.

It has probable recoverable reserves of 20 million barrels and will form the nucleus of the subsequent development of other oil finds in the area, which would extend production by a further six years.

Eighty percent of the project's $75 million capital costs have been met by syndicated foreign loans by Soekor and Energy Africa, and the full capital cost of the project is expected to be recovered within a year of operation.
